title: Detect malicious IDE extension install/usage and IDE tunneling
shortTitle: Detect malicious IDE extension install/usage and IDE tunn...
summary: This strategy covers User Execution or Software Extensions: Malicious IDE Extension, where an attacker publishes or plants an extension for a code editor so that the developer installs and runs it with the editor's own privileges. It matters because integrated development environments, the tools programmers write code in, usually hold credentials, source code, signing keys and network access, so a single extension can reach a large portion of a company's intellectual property. The telemetry that makes it visible is extension installation and update records from the editor and its marketplace, file creation inside the extension directory, process creations whose parent is the editor's extension host, and network connections from editor child processes including tunnelling tools. It fails in practice because developers install extensions freely, most organisations have no allow list, and the malicious behaviour often happens inside the editor's own process tree where ordinary endpoint rules rarely look.

beginner.definition: An integrated development environment is a program where developers write and test code. Extensions are add ons that give it new features. This detection looks for extensions installed from unexpected places, and for the editor starting programs it should not start.
beginner.whyItMatters: The editor already has access to source code, stored credentials and company systems. An extension runs with those same rights. Developers can usually install extensions without asking anyone. One bad extension can quietly copy code or open a remote connection.
howItWorks: The editor records each extension installation and update, including the extension name, version and publisher.
The endpoint agent records files written into the extension folder and programs started by the editor.
The rule looks for extensions installed from a file or a folder instead of the official marketplace.
It also looks for the editor starting network tunnelling tools or command interpreters, which normal editing does not need.
A SIEM, which is a central system that collects and searches log events, joins the installation record with the later process and network activity.
An extension that is both recently installed and starts a tunnel or a script raises a high confidence alert.
beginner.example: Think of a shared kitchen where anyone may add a gadget to the counter. One gadget looks useful, but it also has a small camera pointed at the notice board. Nobody checked the box it came in. This detection inspects the delivery label and watches what each gadget does after it is plugged in.
takeaways: The editor's privileges become the extension's privileges, including any stored credentials.
Watch the extension host process tree, because that is where extension behaviour actually appears.
Marketplace installation is normal, so the signal is off marketplace sources, new publishers and editor started tunnels.

objectives: Explain why code editor extensions are a viable supply chain and execution path.
Identify the installation, file creation and process events that record extension activity.
Recognise editor child processes such as tunnelling tools and interpreters that are abnormal for editing work.
Build an approved extension list per team and alert on off marketplace installations.
Correlate an extension installation with the first process or network connection it produces.
Describe the response steps for a suspicious extension, including removal, credential rotation and code review.
dataSources: Code editor extension installation and update records, including extension identifier, version, publisher and installation source
Endpoint file creation events for files written into the editor extension directory, showing the installing process
Process creation events whose parent image is the code editor or its extension host process, with full command line
Network connection events for the editor and its extension host, including the destination address and port of tunnelling traffic
Software inventory and package manager records listing the approved extensions and their expected publishers for each developer team
logic: The pattern is an extension that was installed from outside the official marketplace, published by a publisher the organisation has never used, or an editor process tree that starts a program which has nothing to do with editing, such as a tunnelling agent, a shell or a remote access binary. You correlate the extension installation record, which gives the identifier, publisher and source, with file creation events inside the extension directory for the same time, with process creation events whose parent is the editor or extension host, and with network connections from those child processes. The malicious case shows a newly installed extension that immediately spawns a command interpreter or a tunnel client, an extension folder containing a compiled native module, or an installation from a downloaded archive or a shared drive. The benign case is a marketplace extension by a well known publisher, installed by the developer, whose child processes are language servers and debuggers with stable paths that appear on many machines.
pseudoQuery:
# title: IDE Extension Installed From Archive Then Spawns Tunnel Client
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventType: 'ide_extension_install'
#     InstallSource|endswith:
#       - '.vsix'
#       - '\\Downloads\\'
#   filter_publisher:
#     Publisher: 'Microsoft'
#   condition: selection and not filter_publisher
# level: medium
falsePositives: Developers installing a company internal extension from a shared build artifact during onboarding
Remote development sessions where the editor starts a secure shell or tunnel process by design to reach a build server
Extension updates that legitimately bundle a language server or debugger with a native module
Simulation or hardware teams installing an off marketplace extension from a vendor download page
Training environments where participants install a prepared extension archive as part of a lab exercise
tuningNotes: Build the filter from two things: the approved publisher list per developer team, and the child process paths that the editor legitimately spawns, such as language servers and debuggers. Alert on off marketplace installation at low severity and on an editor started tunnel, shell or remote access client at high severity, because the second condition is far more specific. Baseline which processes each editor and extension spawns on a sample of developer machines before enabling the process rule, since packaging tools and container helpers will appear. The coverage you lose by trusting approved publishers is a legitimate publisher account being compromised, so keep an alert on any extension update that adds a new child process or network destination the extension has never used before.
